sm: Albert Mohler opens with the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China, noting that the Asia-Pacific region holds much of the world's economic energy and is also a leading zone of military tension, especially the South China Sea. Trump has announced a trade deal with the Philippines, but a deal with China is unlikely to come as quickly. The main event is a three-way meeting of Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, which has no recent precedent. Some say it could ease tensions, while others worry about an elected president sitting with two autocrats who face no term limits, while Trump has about two years left. Mohler contrasts Eastern cyclical views of history with the Western linear view rooted in biblical revelation. He says critics fear Trump's transactional approach, that Trump sees himself as a dealmaker, and that what the leaders say after they go home may matter most.

Mohler turns to former President Joe Biden's 480-page memoir, Promise Me America. He argues Democrats want to forget Biden, and that early liberal reviews are harsh, including a New York Times review saying he fails to own up to his shortcomings. In Mohler's view, the book would be interesting only if Biden admitted that the first 2024 debate showed diminished capacity. The memoir says many people urged him to stay in the race, and Mohler says people around him, including Kamala Harris, must have seen his cognitive decline. He notes a reported 10 million dollar book contract that the publisher may struggle to recoup. Biden also says he was forced out by Democrats and calls Chuck Schumer disloyal, saying loyalty matters to him. Mohler says real loyalty would have meant protecting his dignity.

Mohler discusses a Pew Research Center and CASPAR study, The Future of World Religions, which projects that Muslims will outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035. He calls the research credible and traces Pew's funding to oilman J. Howard Pew. He says this is due to population shifts and differing birth rates, not Christian decline, and that Eastern religions will shrink as birth rates in Asia stay low. China is projected to lose 421 million people. World population is expected to grow 29 percent from 2020 to 2070, with growth of 80 percent among Muslims and 30 percent among Christians. Israel has 6.8 million Jewish citizens, the United States 5.7 million and Europe 1.3 million. Most growth will be in sub-Saharan Africa, where more than half of Christians will live. The Democratic Republic of Congo will have the most Christians, the United States will no longer have a Christian majority, and Buddhist populations in East Asia will drop by more than half.

Mohler marks the death of Lloyd Geering, who died at 108 in New Zealand and was tried for heresy by the Presbyterian Church there in 1967 but found innocent. Geering wrote that the Bible is not the word of God in written form, denied the physical resurrection, and later said he never believed in a personal God. Mohler says Geering late in life predicted New Zealand Christianity would become more conservative because liberals were dying out and not going to church. He reads from the New York Times obituary and quotes Geering urging churches to welcome the secular world. Mohler calls this theological liberalism an attempt to replace Christianity with a different religion while keeping its name, citing J. Gresham Machen. He closes by saying the bodily resurrection is the heart of the faith, and that after this life comes the judgment.
